quest_data.title: Determine Eligibility
quest_data.subtitle: Before filing, confirm that the core eligibility conditions for an IR-1 spouse petition are in place. Complete each section below.

quests.title: Petitioner is a U.S. Citizen
quests.subtitle: Confirm the petitioner qualifies to file an IR-1 spouse petition

screens.label: Petitioner Status
screens.question: What is the petitioner's current immigration status?
screens.helper: The IR-1 visa is only available when the petitioner is a U.S. citizen, not a green card holder.

options.label: U.S. citizen
Lawful Permanent Resident (green card holder)
options.sub: Spouse of LPR uses a different visa category (F2A), not IR-1.

options.label: Not sure
Other / none of these

screens.label: How Citizenship Was Obtained
screens.question: How did the petitioner become a U.S. citizen?
screens.helper: Each path to citizenship is valid for this petition. Pick the one that applies.

options.label: Born in the United States
Born abroad to a U.S. citizen parent (acquired or derived citizenship)
Naturalized (took the oath after immigrating)
Not sure

screens.label: Proof of Citizenship
screens.question: Does the petitioner have at least one accepted proof of U.S. citizenship?
screens.helper: USCIS accepts several document types. You do not need all of them, just one valid proof.

items: Valid, unexpired U.S. passport
U.S. birth certificate issued by a state or county
USCIS Certificate of Naturalization (Form N-550)
USCIS Certificate of Citizenship (Form N-560)
U.S. Consular Report of Birth Abroad (Form FS-240)

options.label: Yes, I have at least one of these documents
Not yet, but I can obtain one
No, and I'm not sure how to get one
Not sure

screens.label: Name Consistency
screens.question: Does the name on the citizenship document match the name the petitioner will use on this petition?
screens.helper: Name discrepancies are manageable with supporting documents. Flag this now so it isn't a surprise later.

options.label: Yes, name matches exactly
No, but I have legal proof of the name change
No, and I don't have name-change proof yet
Not sure

quests.title: A legally valid marriage exists
quests.subtitle: Confirm there is a current, legally recognized civil marriage

screens.label: Relationship Status
screens.question: Which of these best describes the couple's current legal relationship?
screens.helper: USCIS requires an existing, legally recognized civil marriage, not just an engagement or ceremony.

options.label: Legally married (civil registration is in place)
Only engaged, not yet married
Religious or cultural ceremony only, no civil registration
options.sub: Civil registration is typically required for immigration purposes.

options.label: Separated or in the process of divorce
Not sure

screens.label: Legal Recognition
screens.question: Was the marriage legally recognized under the laws of the place where it occurred?
screens.helper: USCIS evaluates marriage validity under the law of the place where it was celebrated. Most civil marriages are valid, but some may have local registration gaps.

options.label: Yes, it was a legally registered civil marriage there
No, it was not legally registered or recognized there
Not sure

screens.label: Marriage Certificate
screens.question: Is there an official marriage certificate or record issued by the appropriate civil authority?
screens.helper: USCIS expects the official civil marriage certificate from the relevant government or registry office, not wedding photos or invitations.

items: Government-issued marriage certificate from the country or state where you married
Certified copy from a civil registry office
Apostille or official authentication if issued abroad

options.label: Yes, I have the official certificate
Not yet, but I can obtain a certified copy
No, and I'm not sure how to get one
Not sure

quests.title: All prior marriages were legally terminated
quests.subtitle: Confirm neither spouse was still married to anyone else when this marriage occurred

screens.label: Prior Marriage History
screens.question: Before this marriage, did either spouse have any previous legally registered marriages?
screens.helper: Count any marriage that was legally registered, anywhere in the world. Religious-only or unregistered ceremonies generally do not count.

options.label: No, neither spouse had any prior legally registered marriages
Yes, the petitioner had a prior marriage
Yes, the beneficiary had a prior marriage
Yes, both had prior marriages
Not sure

screens.label: Termination Timing
screens.question: Did every prior marriage end before the date of the current marriage?
screens.helper: A prior marriage must have ended first, by final divorce, annulment, or the death of the prior spouse, before the new marriage is legally valid.

options.label: Yes, all prior marriages ended before the current marriage
No, at least one prior marriage was still ongoing
Not sure about the exact timing

screens.label: Proof of Termination
screens.question: Is there documentation showing how each prior marriage legally ended?
screens.helper: USCIS will want to see this proof for every prior marriage, for both spouses.

items: Final divorce decree or judgment
Court-issued annulment order
Death certificate of the former spouse

options.label: Yes, documentation exists for all prior marriages
Some, but not all, documentation is missing for at least one
No, no documentation yet
Not sure

quests.title: Marriage is bona fide
quests.subtitle: Screen for good-faith intent and evidence of a genuine relationship

screens.label: Genuine Intent
screens.question: When both spouses married, was it with the genuine intention to build a shared life together?
screens.helper: USCIS looks at whether the marriage was entered in good faith, not primarily for immigration purposes.

options.label: Yes, both intended a genuine marriage
No, immigration was the primary reason for the marriage
I'm not sure how to answer this

screens.label: Relationship Evidence
screens.question: Which of these types of relationship evidence do you currently have?
screens.helper: Select all that apply. Having multiple types of evidence across different categories strengthens the case significantly.

options.label: Shared address or co-habitation history
Joint finances, bank accounts, or shared bills
Photos, travel records, messages, or call logs
Children together, pregnancy, or family evidence
Statements from family, friends, or community who know the couple
None of the above yet

screens.label: Consistency
screens.question: Can both spouses describe the relationship consistently, timeline, how they met, living situation, and future plans?
screens.helper: USCIS interviews often test whether both spouses' stories match on basic facts. This is not about perfection, but about genuine shared knowledge.

options.label: Yes, both are comfortable and consistent on the basics
Mostly, there may be some minor gaps or differences
No, there are significant inconsistencies
Not sure

screens.label: Fraud Risk Flags
screens.question: Are there facts in this case that might raise questions about the relationship's authenticity?
screens.helper: This is just a flag, having a complicating factor doesn't mean the marriage isn't real. It means you'll want to address it proactively.

hint.intro: Common factors that may invite closer review:
items: Very short time between meeting and marriage (a few weeks)
Prior spousal petition filed by either spouse for a different person
Very limited documented contact or time spent together
Significant age difference with limited shared history
Prior finding of marriage fraud in either spouse's immigration history

options.label: No, no significant fraud-risk factors I can think of
Yes, there is at least one factor that may need explanation
Not sure

quests.title: Additional possible visa ineligibilities
quests.subtitle: Early screening for common immigrant visa admissibility concerns

screens.label: Prior Immigration Actions
screens.question: Has the beneficiary ever been refused a U.S. visa, denied an immigration benefit, ordered removed, deported, or accused of using fraud or misrepresentation in any immigration matter?
screens.helper: Prior refusals don't automatically disqualify a case. But fraud or misrepresentation can be a serious bar to admissibility.

options.label: No, none of the above
Yes, at least one of these applies
Not sure

screens.label: Criminal History
screens.question: Does the beneficiary have any arrest, charge, or criminal conviction, anywhere in the world?
screens.helper: Even minor or older matters can affect immigration eligibility. Do not guess or omit, certain convictions can trigger bars to admissibility.

options.label: No, no arrests, charges, or convictions
Yes, there is at least one arrest, charge, or conviction
Not sure

screens.label: Health & Medical
screens.question: Is there any known health issue that might arise during the required immigration medical exam?
screens.helper: The beneficiary must pass a medical exam by a State Department-authorized panel physician at an embassy-approved clinic (consular processing abroad). This screen only asks whether there's a known concern to plan around.

hint.intro: Medical grounds of inadmissibility can include:
items: Certain communicable diseases of public health significance
Failure to have required immigration vaccinations
Certain documented substance use disorders

options.label: No known health concern for the medical exam
Yes, there is a health concern that may come up
Not sure

screens.label: Prior U.S. Immigration History
screens.question: Has the beneficiary ever entered the U.S. without inspection, overstayed a visa, or accumulated unlawful presence in the United States?
screens.helper: Unlawful presence can trigger multi-year or permanent bars to admissibility depending on the amount of time and how departure occurred.

options.label: No, the beneficiary has no such U.S. immigration history
Yes, at least one of these applies
Not sure

screens.label: Financial Sponsorship
screens.question: Is there any concern that meeting the financial sponsorship requirements (Affidavit of Support) may be difficult?
screens.helper: This does not affect eligibility right now, it's a forward-looking flag to plan for. The petitioner will need to meet the minimum income threshold or secure a joint sponsor.

options.label: No known concern, petitioner can likely meet the income requirement
Yes, there may be a challenge meeting the income threshold
Not sure yet

steps.notes: Petitioner must be U.S. citizen (not green card holder). Marriage must be legal and genuine.

risk_signals.disclaimer: Advisory patterns based on USCIS Policy Manual guidance and practitioner-reported RFE trends. Not an official USCIS evaluation rubric.

patterns.title: Marriage under 6 months at filing time
patterns.advisory: USCIS may apply additional scrutiny to short-duration marriages. Strengthen the filing with multiple Tier 1 bona fide evidence items (joint financial accounts, joint tax filings, joint property/lease) and consider including a relationship timeline cover letter.
patterns.source_basis: USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 12, Part G, Ch. 2, bona fide marriage adjudication

patterns.title: Spouses never met in person before marriage
patterns.advisory: Document the communication history thoroughly (call logs, messaging records, video calls) and add a relationship timeline to the petition. Cases involving no in-person meeting commonly face RFEs.
patterns.source_basis: AILA practice advisories; commonly reported RFE pattern

patterns.title: Petitioner previously filed I-130 for a different spouse
patterns.advisory: Under INA Section 204(c), the marriage-fraud bar attaches to the beneficiary, not the petitioner. If the beneficiary was ever found to have entered into (or attempted or conspired to enter into) a marriage to evade the immigration laws, no future petition filed on the beneficiary's behalf may be approved. A petitioner who previously filed for a different spouse is not automatically barred. Consult an immigration attorney before filing.

patterns.title: Prior marriage termination evidence missing
patterns.advisory: If either party had a prior marriage, proof of legal termination is required (divorce decree, annulment order, or death certificate). Without this, USCIS will issue an RFE.

patterns.title: Prior U.S. visa refusal, deportation, or fraud allegation
patterns.advisory: Any prior visa refusal, deportation, removal order, or fraud/misrepresentation allegation must be disclosed and documented in the petition. Misrepresentation under INA 212(a)(6)(C) creates a permanent inadmissibility bar unless waived. Consult an immigration attorney before filing, this is not a DIY scenario.
patterns.source_basis: INA Section 212(a)(6)(C), 8 USC Section 1182(a)(6)(C), misrepresentation bar

patterns.title: Beneficiary has accumulated unlawful presence in the U.S.
patterns.advisory: Unlawful presence triggers the 3-year or 10-year bar under INA 212(a)(9)(B) once the beneficiary departs the U.S. for consular processing. A provisional unlawful presence waiver (Form I-601A) may be required before the visa interview. Consult an immigration attorney to determine the correct path before filing.
patterns.source_basis: INA Section 212(a)(9)(B), 8 USC Section 1182(a)(9)(B), unlawful presence bars

patterns.title: Petitioner income may not meet the 125% poverty guideline
patterns.advisory: The Affidavit of Support (Form I-864) requires the petitioner to demonstrate income at or above 125% of the federal poverty guideline for the household size. If the petitioner cannot meet this on their own, a joint sponsor or qualifying assets will be needed. Plan for this now to avoid an RFE at the NVC stage.
patterns.source_basis: INA Section 213A, 8 USC Section 1183a, Affidavit of Support requirement; Form I-864 instructions

patterns.title: Beneficiary has arrest, charge, or conviction
patterns.advisory: Any arrest, charge, or conviction, anywhere in the world, must be disclosed. A conviction or an admission of a crime involving moral turpitude or a controlled-substance offense may trigger an inadmissibility bar under INA 212(a)(2); an arrest or charge alone generally does not, but must still be documented. Certified court dispositions and police records will be required. Some convictions are waivable; others are permanent bars. Consult an immigration attorney to evaluate impact before filing.
patterns.source_basis: INA Section 212(a)(2), 8 USC Section 1182(a)(2), criminal-related grounds of inadmissibility

filing_data.title: Decide Filing Method

screens.question: Is an attorney or accredited representative managing the filing for you?
screens.helper: If a representative is handling the paperwork, they typically decide the filing method, this walkthrough may not apply.

items: Attorneys can file I-130 online via their USCIS representative account, or by mailing a paper packet, both work
Ask your attorney or document preparer which method they prefer before deciding

options.label: Yes, a representative is handling this
No, I'm filing on my own
Not sure yet

screens.question: Can the petitioner create and manage a USCIS online account?
screens.helper: Online filing requires a free USCIS account at my.uscis.gov, used to complete the form, upload documents, and pay the filing fee.

items: Account setup takes a few minutes and just needs a valid email address
Your USCIS account also delivers notices, requests for evidence, and case updates
Paper filers can add their case to a USCIS account later using the mailed receipt number

options.label: Yes, comfortable setting up and using an online account
No, online accounts aren't practical right now
Not sure

screens.question: Are the required documents available in digital form for upload?
screens.helper: Online filing requires uploading scanned or photographed copies. Paper filing uses physical copies sent by mail.

items: PDF, JPG, or PNG are accepted, a phone camera usually works fine
Documents must be clear and fully legible
A flatbed scanner gives better results for dense documents like a Nikah Nama

options.label: Yes, documents are ready or easy to scan
No, physical copies only, hard to digitize right now
Not sure

screens.question: Does the petitioner have a preference for how to file?
screens.helper: Both methods are fully valid. Your comfort level is a legitimate deciding factor, there is no wrong choice.

options.label: Prefer online, convenient and saves $50
Prefer paper, more comfortable mailing a physical packet
No strong preference, happy with whatever works best

tutorial_steps.label: Step 1 of 10, Sign in to USCIS
tutorial_steps.heading: Sign in to your USCIS account
tutorial_steps.instruction: Go to myaccount.uscis.gov and sign in with the email address and password you set up when creating the account. Complete the two-step verification prompt.
tutorial_steps.note: Two-step verification is required on every login, have your phone or authenticator app ready.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 10, Go to myUSCIS
tutorial_steps.heading: Navigate to myUSCIS
tutorial_steps.instruction: After signing in, you will be directed to the myUSCIS portal homepage. This is your central hub for filing forms, checking case status, and managing your USCIS cases.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 10, MyUSCIS Account Homepage
tutorial_steps.heading: View your account homepage
tutorial_steps.instruction: Your myUSCIS account homepage displays your filed cases, notices, and filing options. This is where you will manage all your online USCIS applications.
tutorial_steps.screenDesc: Your account home and filing hub

tutorial_steps.label: Step 4 of 10, File a Form Online
tutorial_steps.heading: Click 'File a Form Online'
tutorial_steps.instruction: From your account homepage, locate and click the "File a Form Online" button. This is the starting point for all online form submissions.
tutorial_steps.note: If you don't see this button immediately, scroll down, its position may vary on the dashboard.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 5 of 10, Select Form I-130
tutorial_steps.heading: Find and select Form I-130
tutorial_steps.instruction: After clicking "File a Form Online," you will see a list of available forms. Locate Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative and select it to begin.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 6 of 10, Review Filing Methods
tutorial_steps.heading: Confirm your filing method
tutorial_steps.instruction: USCIS may ask you to confirm your filing preference: guided online workflow or PDF upload method. Choose the guided online workflow for step-by-step assistance.
tutorial_steps.screenDesc: Select guided online or PDF upload

tutorial_steps.label: Step 7 of 10, Begin the I-130 Form
tutorial_steps.heading: Start filling out Form I-130
tutorial_steps.instruction: The USCIS portal will walk you through the form section by section. Enter your information carefully, progress saves automatically as you go.
tutorial_steps.note: You can save your progress and return later to continue, the system will remember where you left off.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 8 of 10, Fill Required Fields
tutorial_steps.heading: Complete all required sections
tutorial_steps.instruction: Fill in all required fields carefully and accurately. Your answers must match your official documents. Check twice before moving to the next section.
tutorial_steps.note: Inconsistencies between your form and official documents can lead to a Request for Evidence (RFE), take time to be accurate.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 9 of 10, Go to I-130A Section
tutorial_steps.heading: Complete Form I-130A for beneficiary
tutorial_steps.instruction: After completing the I-130, you will proceed to Form I-130A, the supplemental form for information about the beneficiary (your spouse). Fill this section with your spouse's details.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 10 of 10, Upload I-130A Form
tutorial_steps.heading: Upload the completed I-130A
tutorial_steps.instruction: After completing Form I-130A, upload it along with your supporting evidence. Ensure all files are clearly named, legible, and in PDF or JPG format.
tutorial_steps.note: All documents must be under 12 MB each. Foreign-language documents require certified English translations uploaded separately.

tutorial_steps.note: Review every entry carefully. Changes after signing and payment require contacting USCIS.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 5, Digitally sign the form

tutorial_steps.heading: Proceed to the USCIS payment step

tutorial_steps.caption: The receipt number lets you track your I-130 case status. It also begins the official USCIS processing clock.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Go to the official USCIS fee schedule page
guide_steps.text: Open the official USCIS fee schedule at uscis.gov/g-1055 and select I-130, Petition for Alien Relative from the form dropdown to see the current filing fees. This is the only place you should confirm the fee amount, do not rely on any saved screenshot or old amount.
guide_steps.note: Type 'I-13' in the search field and select 'I-130, Petition for Alien Relative' from the dropdown that appears.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the current I-130 filing fees
guide_steps.text: After selecting I-130, the page shows the current filing fees for Form I-130. Review the fee for Paper Filing before preparing your payment. Have the exact amount ready before assembling the final mailing packet.
guide_steps.note: You are filing by paper, so the applicable fee is the Paper Filing Fee. Prepare payment for this exact amount before packet assembly.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Choose your paper-filing payment method
guide_steps.text:
USCIS no longer accepts personal/business checks, money orders, or cashier's checks. You must use one of the approved payment or fee exemption options:
  • Option A: Pay by credit, debit, or prepaid card using Form G-1450 (Authorization for Credit Card Transactions).
  • Option B: Pay from a U.S. bank account (ACH) using Form G-1650.
  • Option C: If eligible for an exemption from the higher paper filing fee, submit Form G-1651 (Exemption for Paper Fee Payment).
USCIS Form G-1651 Exemption Requirements
To request an exemption, you must certify that electronic payment and collection methods are not possible and you meet 1 or more of the following requirements:
  • You do not have access to banking services or electronic payment systems;
  • Electronic disbursement would cause you undue hardship, as discussed in 31 C.F.R. Part 208;
  • Non-electronic transactions are necessary or desirable for national security or law enforcement reasons; or
  • There are other circumstances as determined by the secretary of the treasury, as reflected in regulations or other guidance.
guide_steps.note: Download and print Form G-1450, Form G-1650, or Form G-1651 from uscis.gov and fill it out completely before placing it in the packet.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Place payment at the front of the packet
guide_steps.text: Once the payment item is ready, whether it is a completed Form G-1450 (card), Form G-1650 (ACH), or Form G-1651 (Fee Exemption), place it at the very front of the mailing packet. The payment or fee exemption form should be the first thing USCIS sees when they open the envelope.

guide_steps.note: Keep the payment form separate and easy to reach so packet assembly in the next step stays quick and organized.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 5

guide_steps.text: Once your payment item is ready, go back to the step card and select your payment method from the dropdown shown in the video above. Saving your selection in Rahvana confirms this step is complete and unlocks the next stage of packet assembly.
guide_steps.note: Payment preparation must be complete before you build the final paper packet. Do not skip this, the packet checklist step depends on it.

guide_steps.title: Assemble Filing Packet
guide_steps.text: Organize the completed paper filing into one final mailing packet before shipment. Place the payment and completed forms at the front, then add supporting evidence and translations behind them in a clean review order. Once everything is stacked, flip through the full packet one more time to confirm nothing is missing and every page is readable before sealing it.
guide_steps.note: Order matters. Payment first, forms next, then supporting documents and translations at the back. A quick final flip-through takes one minute and prevents a missing document from causing a rejection.

steps.step_description: During USCIS review, USCIS may issue a notice requesting additional evidence or information before making a decision. Identify the notice type so Rahvana can guide your specific response.

tool_data.title: USCIS Notice Received
tool_data.subtitle: USCIS may ask for additional evidence or information before deciding your petition. Identify the notice type below so Rahvana can guide your response.

alert.heading: Do not ignore this notice
alert.body: Missing the response deadline can result in your petition being denied — including denial based on abandonment. USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period.

intro_card.heading: Receiving a USCIS notice is not the end of the road
intro_card.body: Most notices give you an opportunity to respond before a final decision is made. The key is to read the notice carefully, respond to exactly what USCIS asked for, and submit a complete response before the deadline.

notice_types.label: I-797 — Approval Notice
notice_types.description: USCIS has approved your I-130 petition and issued an I-797 approval notice. Save the original notice and prepare for the NVC stage.

notice_types.label: RFE — Request for Evidence
notice_types.description: USCIS needs additional evidence or information before it can decide your petition. This is the most common notice. Receiving an RFE does not mean your petition has been denied.

notice_types.label: RFI — Request for Additional Information
notice_types.description: USCIS is asking for clarifying information. Similar in nature to an RFE but typically more limited in scope.

notice_types.label: RFO — Request for Original Document
notice_types.description: USCIS is requesting an original document. You may have submitted a copy where an original is required.

notice_types.label: NOID — Notice of Intent to Deny
notice_types.description: USCIS is considering denying your petition and is giving you a chance to respond. This is more serious than an RFE. Consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

notice_types.label: Denial — I-130 Petition Denied
notice_types.description: USCIS has issued a denial of your I-130 petition. Review the denial notice carefully — it explains the reasons and your available options such as appeal or motion.

notice_types.label: Other USCIS notice or request
notice_types.description: USCIS may send other types of requests such as biometrics appointments or interview notices. Follow the specific instructions on your notice.

where_to_find.title: Where to find your notice

items.detail: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check your case notices and messages. USCIS recommends checking your online account first.
Notices may also be sent by mail to the petitioner's address on file. Keep your address updated with USCIS.

where_to_find.note: If your USCIS online account shows an RFE, an online response portal may be available. Do not mail a duplicate response if you submit online.

deadline_warning.heading: Check the deadline on your actual notice
deadline_warning.body: Do not assume you have a specific number of days. The deadline is printed on your RFE or NOID notice. USCIS states that the maximum response period is generally 12 weeks, but the notice controls the actual deadline for your case.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Evidence · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for Evidence on your I-130 petition. This does not mean your petition is denied — USCIS is giving you an opportunity to provide the evidence needed to decide your case.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFE
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Evidence (RFE) means USCIS needs more information before deciding your petition. This is your opportunity to provide the evidence that closes the gap.

alert.heading: An RFE does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: Receiving an RFE means USCIS is giving you a chance to provide additional evidence before making a final decision. Many petitions are approved after a successful RFE response.

warning_banner.text: Submit your complete RFE response before the deadline printed on your notice. Do not send documents in pieces — USCIS treats a partial response as a request for a decision on the existing record.

common_rfe_reasons.title: Common reasons USCIS issues an I-130 RFE
common_rfe_reasons.subtitle: Read your RFE notice first to identify exactly what USCIS is requesting. The categories below describe common areas — your response should address your specific notice, not all of these.

categories.label: Proof of bona fide marriage
categories.description: USCIS may require stronger evidence that the marriage is genuine and not entered into solely for immigration purposes.
evidence_examples: Photos together (multiple events, locations, over time)
Insurance policies naming spouse as beneficiary
categories.important_note: Do not automatically send all of these. Read exactly what your RFE requests and provide evidence relevant to that specific request.

categories.label: Missing or insufficient relationship documentation
categories.description: USCIS may determine that submitted marriage documentation is insufficient or that additional documents are required.
evidence_examples: Certified English translation of marriage documents
categories.important_note: For Pakistan-based spouses, USCIS may specifically request multiple forms of marriage documentation recognized under Pakistani law.

categories.label: Identity or civil-document issues
categories.description: USCIS may request clarification or supporting documents related to identity or civil records.

categories.label: Inconsistencies between documents
categories.description: If dates, spellings, or other details differ across documents such as your passport, CNIC, Nikah Nama, NADRA certificate, and I-130, USCIS may request clarification.
evidence_examples: Certified document showing the correct information
categories.important_note: Name spelling variations and date discrepancies across Pakistani identity documents are common. Address them directly and specifically in your response.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Don't panic — read your RFE first
guide_steps.text: An RFE does not mean your petition is denied. USCIS is asking for additional evidence before making a decision. Your first task is to obtain the actual RFE notice and read it carefully — every word of it.
guide_steps.note: Get the notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. The online account is the recommended first place to check.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Identify exactly what USCIS is requesting
guide_steps.text: Do not randomly gather documents. The RFE will specifically identify what is deficient and what USCIS needs. Your response must directly address the specific issue identified in the RFE — nothing more, nothing less.
guide_steps.note: For example: 'Submit evidence demonstrating that the marriage between the petitioner and beneficiary is bona fide' is different from 'Submit a certified English translation of the marriage certificate.' Each requires a different response.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Check the deadline printed on your notice
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your RFE notice. Do not assume you have a specific number of days — the actual notice controls your deadline. USCIS policy states that extensions beyond the permitted response period are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Mark the deadline in your calendar immediately. Build in time to organize, review, and submit your response well before the deadline.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Organize your evidence by RFE request
guide_steps.text: Structure your evidence to match each item USCIS requested. Group documents under the specific request they address. For example — USCIS Request: Proof of bona fide marriage: Exhibit A — Marriage certificate, Exhibit B — Photos, Exhibit C — Travel records, Exhibit D — Communication evidence, Exhibit E — Joint financial records. This structure makes it easy for the USCIS officer to match your response to their request.
guide_steps.note: Clear organization significantly helps the reviewing officer understand your response and reduces the chance of important evidence being overlooked.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Write a cover letter
guide_steps.text: Prepare a brief cover letter that explains: (1) what USCIS requested, (2) how your response addresses each specific request, and (3) what evidence is included and how it is organized. The cover letter is the roadmap for your response package.
guide_steps.note: The cover letter does not need to be lengthy. It should clearly summarize the response contents and make it easy for the officer to navigate your package.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 6
guide_steps.title: Assemble one complete response package
guide_steps.text: Gather your cover letter and all evidence together into one complete response package before submitting. USCIS policy states that when responding to an RFE, materials should generally be submitted together. A partial response is treated as a request for a decision on the record — USCIS does not wait for additional packages or issue another RFE.
guide_steps.note: Double-check that every document is included, every translation is certified, and the cover letter is accurate before you submit.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 7
guide_steps.title: Choose the correct submission method
guide_steps.text: Check whether your USCIS online account provides an RFE response portal for your case. If it does, follow the online submission instructions. If your case requires a mailed response, use the address and instructions specified in your RFE notice.
guide_steps.note: USCIS has specifically stated that users who respond online should NOT also mail a duplicate response. Follow the method indicated on your notice or in your USCIS account.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 8
guide_steps.title: Keep a complete copy of everything you submit
guide_steps.text: Before submitting, make copies of your complete response package, including the cover letter and all evidence. If submitting by mail, use a trackable carrier and save the tracking number. If submitting online, save a copy of the confirmation.
guide_steps.note: Your copy of the response is important if questions arise later about what was submitted and when.

citations.text: USCIS Policy Manual - Request For Evidence

after_submission.heading: After you submit your RFE response
after_submission.body: Your case returns to USCIS review. USCIS will consider the submitted evidence and issue one of these outcomes.

outcomes.label: Approval
outcomes.description: USCIS approves the I-130 petition. For consular processing, the case moves toward the National Visa Center (NVC) stage.

outcomes.label: Denial
outcomes.description: If the response does not establish eligibility, USCIS may deny the petition. The denial notice will explain available appeal and motion options.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If your RFE involves complex legal issues or you are uncertain how to respond, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Additional Information · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for Additional Information (RFI) on your I-130 petition. An RFI typically requests clarifying information and is generally narrower in scope than an RFE.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFI
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Additional Information (RFI) means USCIS needs specific clarifying information before proceeding. Read the notice carefully and respond directly to what is asked.

alert.heading: An RFI does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: USCIS is requesting clarifying information to continue processing your petition. Respond to exactly what is asked, before the deadline printed on the notice.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the RFI notice
guide_steps.text: Check your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or your physical mail for the RFI notice. Read the notice carefully to understand exactly what information USCIS is requesting.
guide_steps.note: An RFI is typically narrower in scope than an RFE. USCIS is asking for specific clarifying information, not a broad set of evidence.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFI notice. Note it immediately and plan your response with enough time to review everything before submitting.
guide_steps.note: USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period. Missing the deadline can result in a denial.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Prepare a clear, direct response
guide_steps.text: Respond directly to the information USCIS requested. Provide only what is asked — clear, focused, and accurate. Include a brief cover letter that identifies what was requested and how your response addresses it.
guide_steps.note: Clarity is key. A focused response that directly answers the question is more effective than a large unorganized package.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response into a single submission. Do not submit in pieces. Use the submission method specified in your RFI notice — online portal if available in your USCIS account, or mail if instructed.
guide_steps.note: If submitting online, do not also mail a duplicate response. Keep a copy of everything you submit.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you are uncertain about your RFI response, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Original Document · Locate & submit original
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for an Original (RFO) document. USCIS is requesting that you submit the original version of a document you may have previously submitted as a copy.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFO
guide_data.subtitle: USCIS is requesting an original document. Identify the specific document requested, locate the original, and submit it following the instructions on your notice.

alert.heading: USCIS is asking for an original, not a copy
alert.body: Carefully read your RFO notice to identify exactly which document is required in original form. Submitting another copy will not satisfy the request.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Identify the specific document requested
guide_steps.text: Read your RFO notice carefully. USCIS will identify the specific document it is requesting in original form. Common examples include original marriage certificates, original Nikah Namas, or other original civil documents.
guide_steps.note: If you are unsure whether your document is truly the original versus a certified copy, contact the issuing authority to clarify.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFO notice. Mark it immediately. Plan enough time to locate the document, make a copy for your records, and prepare your submission.
guide_steps.note: Do not wait until close to the deadline. Locating original documents, especially civil documents from Pakistan, may take time.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Make a copy before submitting the original
guide_steps.text: Before sending any original document to USCIS, make a clear copy for your own records. USCIS receives many documents and originals are not always returned promptly, or may take significant time to be returned.
guide_steps.note: Keep your copy in a safe place. If the original is irreplaceable, consider consulting an immigration attorney about the best approach.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit using a secure, trackable method
guide_steps.text: Send the original document using a secure and trackable shipping method. Include a cover letter identifying the case receipt number, the RFO reference, and what document is enclosed. Follow the submission instructions in your RFO notice.
guide_steps.note: Keep the tracking number and delivery confirmation. Once the carrier shows delivered, save that proof.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you have concerns about submitting irreplaceable original documents, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Notice of Intent to Deny · Respond carefully before deadline
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) on your I-130 petition. A NOID is more serious than an RFE — USCIS is indicating it is considering denying your petition based on the current record and is giving you one opportunity to respond.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS NOID
guide_data.subtitle: A Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) means USCIS is considering denying your petition. This is your opportunity to respond with evidence and legal arguments before a final decision is made.

alert.heading: A NOID is more serious than an RFE
alert.body: USCIS is not simply asking for more evidence. It is indicating that based on the current record, it intends to deny your petition — and is giving you one opportunity to respond. Carefully review the reasons USCIS has stated. Because the response may require legal analysis, strongly consider getting help from a qualified immigration attorney.

noid_vs_rfe.title: NOID vs. RFE — the key difference

rfe.label: RFE
rfe.description: We need more evidence before we can make a decision.

noid.label: NOID
noid.description: Based on what we currently have, we are considering denying your petition. Here is why. You have one opportunity to respond.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the NOID notice immediately
guide_steps.text: Obtain the NOID notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. Read the entire notice carefully. USCIS is required to identify the intended reasons for denial, explain deficiencies, and identify potentially missing evidence.
guide_steps.note: Understanding exactly what USCIS says is wrong is the foundation of your response. Do not skip or skim any part of the notice.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline immediately
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your NOID notice. Note it immediately and treat it as your hard deadline. Extensions are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Given the seriousness of a NOID, you should begin working on your response immediately — do not wait until close to the deadline.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Because a NOID response may require legal analysis and argumentation — not just evidence submission — strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney before preparing your response. An attorney can assess the specific deficiencies USCIS identified and advise on the best response strategy.
guide_steps.note: This is Rahvana's strongest recommendation for NOID situations. The consequences of a denial are significant — the response deserves careful legal attention.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Address each stated reason for the proposed denial
guide_steps.text: Your response must directly address each reason USCIS stated in the NOID. For each issue identified, explain why that reason does not support denial and provide evidence that counters or clarifies the issue.
guide_steps.note: A NOID response is not just an evidence package — it should include a legal argument explaining why, based on the law and facts, the petition should be approved.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response before the deadline
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response — cover letter, legal arguments, and all supporting evidence — into a single submission. Follow the submission instructions on your NOID notice. Do not send documents in pieces.
guide_steps.note: Keep a complete copy of everything you submit, with proof of submission (tracking number or online confirmation).

after_noid_response.heading: After submitting your NOID response
after_noid_response.body: USCIS will review your response and issue a final decision.

outcomes.label: Approval
outcomes.description: USCIS approves the petition based on your response. The case moves toward the NVC stage for consular processing.

outcomes.label: Denial
outcomes.description: If the response does not establish eligibility, USCIS will deny the petition. The denial notice will explain available appeal and motion options such as an appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals.

citations.text: USCIS Policy Manual - Notice of Intent to Deny

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. A NOID is a serious notice that may require legal analysis. Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_description: Your response to the USCIS notice has been submitted. The case is back in USCIS review. Monitor case status and be prepared for the possible outcomes.

tool_data.title: Awaiting USCIS Decision
tool_data.subtitle: Your response has been submitted. USCIS is now reviewing your response alongside the original petition. Monitor your case status and be ready for the next update.

status_card.heading: Response submitted — USCIS is reviewing
status_card.body: After receiving your response, USCIS will review the submitted evidence and issue a decision. There is no set timeline for this review. Continue monitoring your case status.

possible_outcomes.label: Approval
possible_outcomes.description: USCIS approves your I-130 petition. For a spouse living outside the U.S. pursuing consular processing, the case generally moves to the National Visa Center (NVC) stage. USCIS sends the approved petition to the Department of State/NVC.

possible_outcomes.label: Denial
possible_outcomes.description: If the response does not establish eligibility, USCIS may deny the petition. Review the denial notice carefully — it will explain the specific reasons and what appeal or motion options may be available.

possible_outcomes.label: Further Action
possible_outcomes.description: In some cases, USCIS may issue additional requests before making a final decision. Continue monitoring your USCIS online account.

monitoring_tips: Check your USCIS online account regularly for status updates.
Keep a copy of your submitted response accessible in case it is needed again.
If USCIS issues a denial, the denial notice will explain available appeal or motion options.
Use the waiting period to stay prepared for the NVC stage in case the petition is approved.
tool_data.footer_note: Rahvana will help you navigate the next step based on the outcome USCIS provides.

steps.step_description: USCIS has denied the I-130 petition. Review the denial notice carefully to understand the specific reasons and determine which options — appeal, motion, or another strategy — may be appropriate for your situation.

guide_data.title: I-130 Denied — Review Your Options
guide_data.subtitle: An I-130 denial is a serious outcome, but it may not be the end of the road. Review the denial notice carefully and understand what options may be available.

alert.heading: Carefully review the denial notice
alert.body: The denial notice explains USCIS's specific reasons for the denial and states what appeal or motion options are available in your case. The correct next step depends entirely on the specific reasons for the denial and the facts of your case. Do not file an appeal or motion without understanding the denial first.

denial_options.title: Possible options after an I-130 denial
denial_options.subtitle: Which option is appropriate depends on the specific reasons for the denial and the circumstances of your case. The denial notice itself explains what options are available.

options.label: Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
options.description: Certain I-130 decisions can be appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals using Form EOIR-29 (Notice of Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals from a Decision of a DHS Officer). USCIS confirms that I-130 appeals are among the appeals filed using Form EOIR-29.
options.important: Appeals have strict deadlines. Check your denial notice for the deadline and the specific appeal procedure that applies to your case.

options.label: Motion to Reopen
options.description: A motion to reopen asks USCIS to reopen the case based on new facts or evidence that was not available at the time of the decision.
options.important: A motion to reopen is appropriate when there is new factual evidence that was not part of the original record. Review the denial carefully before pursuing this option.

options.label: Motion to Reconsider
options.description: A motion to reconsider asks USCIS to reconsider its decision based on an error of law or incorrect application of policy to the existing facts.
options.important: A motion to reconsider is appropriate when you believe USCIS made a legal error in the denial, not when you simply have new evidence.

options.label: File a new petition
options.description: Depending on the denial reason, it may sometimes be appropriate to file a new I-130 petition with corrected information or additional evidence. This should be carefully evaluated based on the specific denial reason.
options.important: Filing a new petition when an appeal or motion is more appropriate may not be the best strategy. Consult an immigration attorney.

attorney_recommendation.heading: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
attorney_recommendation.body: Determining the right strategy after an I-130 denial — appeal vs. motion vs. new petition — requires careful analysis of the denial reasons, the evidence record, and the applicable law. The wrong choice can waste time, resources, or foreclose other options. An experienced immigration attorney can help you evaluate the best path forward.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the denial notice completely
guide_steps.text: The denial notice contains the specific reasons USCIS denied the petition and explains what appeal or motion rights are available. Read it completely before deciding on any next step.
guide_steps.note: The denial notice is the most important document at this stage. Every option you consider must be evaluated against the specific reasons stated in the notice.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines for appeal or motion
guide_steps.text: If the denial notice indicates appeal or motion rights, it will also state the deadlines for filing. These deadlines are strict — missing them can eliminate certain options.
guide_steps.note: Do not delay in reviewing the notice and understanding the available deadlines. Begin consulting an attorney as soon as possible if you are considering an appeal or motion.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Consult a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Given the complexity of determining the right post-denial strategy, consulting a qualified immigration attorney is strongly recommended. An attorney can review the denial notice, assess the options, and advise on the best course of action specific to your case.
guide_steps.note: Do not treat this as optional. The stakes of an I-130 denial are high, and the correct path forward requires professional evaluation.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Evaluate and act on the appropriate option
guide_steps.text: Based on the denial reasons and legal advice, determine whether an appeal (Form EOIR-29 to the BIA), a motion to reopen, a motion to reconsider, or another strategy is appropriate. Act within the applicable deadlines.
guide_steps.note: Rahvana can guide you through general information about each option, but the final decision on which path to take should be made with qualified legal assistance.

alert.heading: Identify the Form Number and Heading
alert.body: Official USCIS notices are usually issued on Form I-797C (Notice of Action) or Form I-797. Look at the top-right header and notice type line to understand whether action is required or if it is purely informational.

common_rfe_reasons.title: Common notice types you may receive
common_rfe_reasons.subtitle: USCIS sends several standard communication types. Find your notice type below:

categories.label: Biometrics / ASC Appointment Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: USCIS schedules an appointment at an Application Support Center (ASC) to capture fingerprints, photo, and signature. This is common if biometric verification is needed.
evidence_examples: Bring the original appointment notice with barcode.
Bring government-issued photo ID (valid passport, driver's license).
If you cannot attend, follow the reschedule instructions on the notice immediately before the appointment date.
categories.important_note: Failing to appear for a biometrics appointment without rescheduling can result in petition abandonment and denial.

categories.label: Interview Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: While most consular I-130 petitions are decided without an in-person USCIS interview, USCIS occasionally requests a domestic petitioner interview or joint interview.
evidence_examples: Original civil documents (marriage certificate, birth certificates).
Updated proof of ongoing bona fide marriage (recent joint bills, photos, financial statements).
categories.important_note: Carefully review the checklist of items to bring on the interview notice and arrive 15 minutes before the scheduled time.

categories.label: Service Center Transfer Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: USCIS frequently transfers cases between service centers (e.g., Nebraska, Texas, Potomac, California, Vermont) to balance processing workloads across the agency.
evidence_examples: No action is required on your part.
Future correspondence will come from the new service center.
categories.important_note: A case transfer does not mean anything is wrong with your petition. It is routine workload management by USCIS.

categories.label: Fee Correction / Rejection Notice
categories.description: If payment could not be processed or an essential document was missing at intake, USCIS issues a notice explaining the intake issue.
evidence_examples: Check the specific rejection reason printed on the notice.
Submit corrected fee payment or missing signature promptly.
Ensure payment instrument (check, credit card authorization Form G-1450) is valid and funded.
categories.important_note: Pay close attention to any refiling instructions and deadline dates provided on the notice.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the entire notice thoroughly
guide_steps.text: Check the notice type in the header, read all instructions, and verify whether USCIS requires a response, an appearance, or if the notice is purely informational.
guide_steps.note: Look for specific keywords such as 'Action Required', 'Notice of Action', or 'Appointment Scheduled'.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check your USCIS online account
guide_steps.text: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check the 'Documents' tab for an electronic PDF copy of the notice. Online notices are often available days before physical mail arrives.
guide_steps.note: Ensure your mailing address in your USCIS account is completely accurate and up to date.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines or appointment dates
guide_steps.text: If the notice specifies an appointment date, time, and location, or gives a deadline to submit documents, mark it on your calendar immediately.
guide_steps.note: Never wait until the last week. If rescheduling is needed, USCIS generally requires requests to be submitted well ahead of the appointment date.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Comply with the exact instructions and retain proof
guide_steps.text: Attend the appointment or submit the requested documentation according to the exact mailing or online upload instructions. Keep copies of everything submitted, along with delivery tracking numbers or stamped appointment notices.
guide_steps.note: Save your stamped biometrics confirmation sheet or mailing receipt in your immigration records binder.

tool_data.subtitle: Review and prepare the civil documents needed for NVC / CEAC document upload and later consular interview readiness.

items.title: Beneficiary Passport Biographic Page
items.sub: Current passport page showing photo and personal details

items.title: Birth Certificate
items.sub: Beneficiary's civil birth record

items.title: Marriage Certificate / Marriage Registration Record
items.sub: Official civil proof of the marriage, Nikah Nama and NADRA MRC

sections.c: For Pakistan-origin cases, this typically means both the Nikah Nama (the Islamic marriage contract) and the NADRA Marriage Registration Certificate (MRC). Both together form the complete civil marriage record.
The marriage record should align with what was submitted during the I-130 USCIS stage. Ensure names, dates, and spelling are consistent.
The Nikah Nama (in Urdu) requires a full certified English translation. The NADRA MRC is bilingual but may still require a certified translation for CEAC upload.
Older Nikah Namas may have faded or handwritten entries. Ensure scans are fully legible before upload.

items.title: Police Certificate
items.sub: Pakistan Police Character Certificate (PCC) for the beneficiary

items.title: Certified English Translations
items.sub: Required for all non-English civil documents

sections.c: Every document not in English must be accompanied by a full certified English translation. This applies to all stages, USCIS, NVC, and consular.
A certification statement from the translator attesting that they are competent to translate from the source language to English and that the translation is accurate and complete.
Upload the original document and its translation as separate files or clearly labeled together. CEAC expects both, original and translation, for each non-English document.
Do not translate only part of a document. The entire document must be translated. Partial translations may trigger an RFE or document request from NVC.

items.title: Prior Marriage Termination Documents
items.sub: Required if either spouse was previously married

sections.c: If either the petitioner or beneficiary was previously married, CEAC will require proof that every prior marriage legally ended before the current marriage.

• Final divorce decree or judgment
  • Annulment order
  • Death certificate of former spouse

For talaq in Pakistan: the divorce is not legally effective until the 90-day reconciliation period expires and the Union Council issues the final divorce certificate. Ensure you have the final certificate, not just the initial notice.
All termination documents in Urdu must be accompanied by certified English translations.

items.title: Death Certificate of Former Spouse
items.sub: Only if prior marriage ended by death

sections.c: Required only if a prior marriage ended because of the death of the former spouse. A death certificate from the appropriate civil authority is needed.
If in Urdu or another language, a certified English translation is required alongside the original.

items.title: Name Change Documents
items.sub: Legal proof of any name change used in the case

sections.c: If the beneficiary's name in the passport or marriage record differs from the name used in other documents due to a legal name change, documentation of that change is required.

• Court order for name change
  • Marriage certificate showing a change of surname

items.title: Missing Document / Record Unavailability Evidence
items.sub: When a required record genuinely does not exist

sections.c: If a required document, such as a birth certificate or civil record, is genuinely unavailable or was never issued, substitute documentation may be submitted.

• A statement from the relevant civil authority confirming the record does not exist
  • Secondary evidence supporting the missing fact (hospital records, school records, etc.)
  • Personal affidavit explaining the circumstances
Missing-document submissions require careful handling. Consult an immigration attorney if a key civil record is unavailable before uploading substitutes.

items.title: Organized Translation Set
items.sub: All translations paired and labeled with their originals

sections.c: Keeping each original and its certified translation clearly paired and labeled reduces the chance of upload errors in CEAC and makes case review easier.

• Name each file pair clearly: e.g., "NikahNama_Original.pdf" and "NikahNama_Translation.pdf"
  • Group translations by person and document type before upload

items.title: Upload-Ready File Copies
items.sub: Clean, legible, properly formatted scan set

sections.c: CEAC has a 4 MB file size limit per upload. Files must be clear, legible, and properly cropped with no missing edges.

• Use consistent file naming across the packet
  • Verify each file opens correctly and is fully readable
  • PDF format is generally preferable for multi-page documents
If files are larger than 4 MB, use Rahvana's Document Vault compression tool to bring them within the CEAC upload limit.

items.title: Relationship Evidence Backup Set
items.sub: Supporting bona fide marriage evidence for later use

sections.c: While relationship evidence is not a core NVC civil document, having an organized backup set ready ensures you are prepared for any document requests or interview questions about the marriage.

• Photos together (wedding and casual, across different dates)
  • Communication history samples
  • Travel/visit documentation
  • Financial ties or joint records

financial_requirements.disclaimer: Affidavit of Support thresholds are set by the annual HHS Poverty Guidelines and Form I-864 instructions. Figures below are the rule structure, not a specific year's dollar amounts.
guidance: Required income is 125% of the HHS Poverty Guideline for the sponsor's household size (100% if the petitioner is active-duty military sponsoring a spouse).
Household size includes the sponsor, dependents, the intending immigrant, and anyone previously sponsored.
Assets may cover an income shortfall, generally valued at 3x the gap (5x for some categories).
Each sponsor files a separate I-864.

tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Resubmit corrected financial document

steps.step_description: Attend your scheduled medical examination with an embassy-approved panel physician. This is a mandatory health screening and vaccination review for all immigrants.

bring: Relevant medical records and test results for major illnesses, surgeries, or current treatment, if applicable

steps.step_description: Assemble the original hard-copy documents needed for your consular interview. Review each item and organize your packet carefully before interview day.

items.title: Passport (current + any prior passports)
items.sub: Bring originals of all passports, current and expired, that contain U.S. visa history

sections.c: Bring the original current passport with at least 6 months validity beyond the interview date. If applicable, bring previous passports containing relevant U.S. immigration or travel history.
Bring one photocopy of the biographic page of each passport in a separate section from the originals.

items.title: Original Birth Certificate
items.sub: Beneficiary's official civil birth record

sections.c:
Bring the original Birth Registration Certificate issued by the authority responsible for registering the beneficiary's birth:

  • Union Council
  • Municipal Corporation
  • Capital Development Authority (CDA) — Islamabad
  • Cantonment Board

Select the issuing authority that applies to your birth record and bring the original document.

If a Birth Registration Certificate is unavailable, the following NADRA documents may serve as alternate documents:

  • Child Registration Certificate (CRC/B-Form)
  • Family Registration Certificate (FRC)
If your birth document is in Urdu, bring the original Urdu document together with the required certified English translation.

items.title: Original Marriage Certificate / Nikah Nama
items.sub: Original Nikah Nama and NADRA MRC, plus translations

sections.c: Bring your original Marriage Registration Certificate (MRC), English translation, and photocopy. Also bring your original Nikah Nama and English translation if applicable/available, particularly as supporting evidence of the marriage.
Do not submit photocopies at the window unless asked. Bring originals first and let the consular officer direct you.

items.title: Original Police Clearance Certificate (Fresh)
items.sub: The fresh PCC obtained for this interview cycle

sections.c: Bring the original fresh PCC obtained during Chapter 3 Step 3. Do not bring the older PCC submitted during NVC processing, this must be the fresh one.
Confirm the PCC is still within the validity window for your embassy. Some posts specify a maximum age for the PCC at interview.

items.title: Interview Appointment Letter
items.sub: The original printed NVC interview appointment letter

sections.c: Print and bring the original interview appointment letter received from NVC. This is your primary identification for entry into the embassy grounds.

items.title: Original Affidavit of Support, Petitioner
items.sub: Original signed I-864 or I-864EZ from the petitioner

sections.c: Bring the original signed Affidavit of Support. This must be the wet-ink signed original, not a photocopy.

items.title: DS-260 Confirmation Page
items.sub: Online Immigrant Visa Application Confirmation

sections.c: Bring the printed DS-260 confirmation page with barcode. This confirms you have successfully submitted your online immigrant visa application.
Make sure all information in your DS-260 form is accurate and matches your supporting documents such as passport and civil records.
You can download and print the confirmation page after submitting your DS-260 form from the Consular Electronic Application Center (CEAC) website.

items.title: Most Recent Tax Evidence, Petitioner
items.sub: Federal tax return or IRS transcript copies

sections.c: Bring copies of the most recent year's tax return or IRS transcript. Originals are not always required, copies are generally acceptable, but bring them organized.

items.title: Employment Letter, Petitioner
items.sub: Current employment confirmation letter if available

sections.c: If the petitioner's current employer can provide an employment letter, bring it as supporting evidence of current income. Not always required but useful to have.

items.title: Passport-Style Photos
items.sub: 2-4 recent passport-style photos meeting embassy specifications

sections.c: Bring 2-4 recent passport-style photos. Check your specific embassy's photo requirements for size and background specifications. US Embassy Pakistan typically requires standard 2x2 inch photos.

items.title: Polio Vaccination Certificate (Original)
items.sub: The original polio vaccination certificate from an approved site

sections.c: Bring the original polio vaccination certificate obtained in Step 2. The panel physician should have already reviewed it, but bring the original in case it is requested at the window.

items.title: Medical Examination Results Packet Reference
items.sub: Not brought by you, sealed by physician, but confirm it was sent

sections.c: The medical examination results are sealed by the panel physician and sent directly to the embassy. You do not carry the medical packet yourself. Confirm with your physician that the results were submitted before your interview date.

items.title: Courier Registration Certificate
items.sub: Proof of courier service registration for passport delivery

sections.c: Bring a printed copy of your courier registration confirmation. This shows where your passport and visa will be delivered after approval.
Ensure the selected courier location and contact details are correct. Any mistake may delay the delivery of your passport.
You can register and download your courier confirmation from the official portal: Register Courier Service.

items.title: Labeled Folder System or Document Binder
items.sub: Organized tabs separating each document group

sections.c: A well-organized packet makes it easier to quickly produce any document the officer requests. Disorganized packets slow down the interview and create unnecessary stress.

• Use a clear-pocket binder or labeled folder tabs
  • Label each section clearly: Passport / Civil / Financial / Extras
  • Keep originals in one section, copies in another

items.title: Full Photocopy Set of All Documents
items.sub: One complete photocopy set kept separate from originals

sections.c: Consular officers may retain copies of certain documents. Having a pre-prepared copy set means you don't risk giving away originals unnecessarily.

tutorial.heading: The consular interview window
tutorial.instruction: You will be called to a consular window. The officer will review your documents, ask questions about your relationship, background, and immigration history. Answer concisely and truthfully. Do not volunteer information beyond what is asked.
tutorial.note: Consistency is critical. Your answers must align with your DS-260 responses and the documents you submitted during NVC processing.
tutorial.visual:
Common interview questions
How did you meet your spouse?
When and where was your marriage?
What does your petitioner do for work?
Have you visited the United States before?
Where will you live in the United States?

tutorial.label: Step 6 of 8
tutorial.heading: Document review at the window
tutorial.instruction: The officer may ask you to produce specific original documents. Present them calmly and in the order requested. Having a well-organized packet makes this faster and smoother.
tutorial.visual:
Be ready to produce
Original passport(s)
Marriage certificate / Nikah Nama
Birth certificate
Police clearance certificate
Affidavit of Support
Passport photos

tutorial.label: Step 7 of 8
tutorial.heading: Stay calm, the officer is doing their job
tutorial.instruction: Consular officers ask direct questions. Their tone is professional, not personal. Nervousness is expected and normal. Answer clearly and calmly. If you do not understand a question, politely ask for clarification.
tutorial.visual: Answer only what is asked. Be honest. Be calm. Be concise. You have prepared for this, trust your preparation.

tutorial.label: Step 8 of 8
tutorial.heading: Possible outcomes after the interview
tutorial.instruction: The officer will indicate the outcome at the window or shortly after. The three main outcomes are approval, Administrative Processing (AP), or refusal. If AP applies, proceed to Step 9 to track and manage the AP process.
tutorial.visual:
What you may hear
Approved, passport retained, visa to be delivered Best
Administrative Processing, more time needed Step 9
Refused, written reason provided Consult attorney

checklists.title: What to bring
items: Interview appointment letter (printed original)
Current passport (original)
All prior passports
Original civil documents (organized packet)
2 recent color photographs (5 cm × 5 cm / 2 × 2 in)
Petitioner's original Affidavit of Support
Tax evidence and employment letter if applicable

checklists.title: Common pitfalls
items: Arriving without the printed appointment letter
Bringing electronic devices that are prohibited beyond security
Disorganized packet, makes document retrieval slow and stressful
Inconsistent answers, not matching DS-260 responses
Volunteering extra information that was not asked
Arriving late, embassy entry is strictly time-controlled

tips: Arrive 20-30 minutes before your appointment time
Keep your document packet organized with labeled tabs
Answer only what is asked, concisely and truthfully
Stay calm, nervousness is normal and expected
Have originals on top and copies in a separate section
If unsure of an answer, say so calmly, do not guess

outcomes.sub: The officer approves the visa. Your passport will be held and the visa will be delivered via the courier service you registered.

outcomes.label: Administrative Processing (AP / 221g)
outcomes.sub: The officer needs more time or additional documents. This is not a refusal. Proceed to Step 9 to track and manage the AP process.

outcomes.label: Visa refused
outcomes.sub: The officer denies the visa under a specific ground. A refusal typically comes with a written reason. Consult an immigration attorney if this occurs.

explainer.title: The embassy needs specific documents from you
explainer.body: A 221(g) notice is not a final refusal. The officer requires additional documents or information before a decision can be made. Gather exactly what was requested, submit via the method stated in the notice, and log your submission below. Once submitted, your case moves into consular review.

info_sections.title: How to respond to a 221(g)
items: Submit exactly what was requested, nothing more, nothing less
If the notice specifies a method (drop box, mail, email), use that method
If the notice specifies a deadline, meet it, do not delay
Keep a complete copy of everything you submit
After submission, check CEAC weekly for status changes
Monitor the email registered with the consulate for any follow-up

info_sections.title: What happens after submission
items: After submission, the case typically moves to Administrative Processing while the consulate reviews what you sent
CEAC may show 'Administrative Processing' during this period
Resolution timelines vary, from days to several months depending on the case
If approved after 221(g) review, your passport will be delivered via the courier you registered

info_sections.title: What to do while waiting
items: Check your CEAC status approximately once a week and record any changes.
Monitor the email address registered with the embassy for additional requests or updates.
Respond promptly if the embassy requests further documents or information.
Ensure your passport remains valid throughout the review process.
If your case remains pending significantly longer than normal, follow your embassy's official inquiry instructions before contacting them.
